entries.b9d1b2749560904f9db617a34ecc653df458590f: <div sID="gen12556" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="114" osisID="Ps.114" sID="Ps.114"/> <div eID="gen12556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12557" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12558" type="x-p"/> The deliverance of Israel out of Egypt gave birth to their church and nation, which were then founded, then formed; that work of wonder ought therefore to be had in everlasting remembrance. God gloried in it, in the preface to the ten commandments, and <reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">Hos. xi. 1</reference>, "Out of Egypt have I called my son." In this psalm it is celebrated in lively strains of praise; it was fitly therefore made a part of the great Hallelujah, or song of praise, which the Jews were wont to sing at the close of the passover-supper. It must never be forgotten, I. That they were brought out of slavery, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. That God set up his tabernacle among them, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.2">ver. 2</reference>. III. That the sea and Jordan were divided before them, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.3">ver. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.5">5</reference>. IV. That the earth shook at the giving of the law, when God came down on Mount Sinai, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.4">ver. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.6">6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.7">7</reference>. V. That God gave them water out of the rock, <reference osisRef="Ps.114.8">ver. 8</reference>. In singing this psalm we must acknowledge God's power and goodness in what he did for Israel, applying it to the much greater work of wonder, our redemption by Christ, and encouraging ourselves and others to trust in God in the greatest straits.
entries.da291348681faba3540c2c2172fc6caa09bdc286: <div eID="gen12558" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12557" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Deliverance of Israel Celebrated.</title> <div sID="gen12559" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language; <hi type="super">2</hi> Judah was his sanctuary, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Israel his dominion. <hi type="super">3</hi> The sea saw <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and fled: Jordan was driven back. <hi type="super">4</hi> The mountains skipped like rams, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the little hills like lambs. <hi type="super">5</hi> What <hi type="italic">ailed</hi> thee, O thou sea, that thou fleddest? thou Jordan, <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou wast driven back? <hi type="super">6</hi> Ye mountains, <hi type="italic">that</hi> ye skipped like rams; <hi type="italic">and</hi> ye little hills, like lambs? <hi type="super">7</hi> Tremble, thou earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob; <hi type="super">8</hi> Which turned the rock <hi type="italic">into</hi> a standing water, the flint into a fountain of waters. <div eID="gen12559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12560" type="x-p"/> The psalmist is here remembering <hi type="italic">the days of old, the years of the right hand of the Most High,</hi> and the wonders which their fathers told them of (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.13">Judg. vi. 13</reference>), for time, as it does not wear out the guilt of sin, so it should not wear out the sense of mercy. Let it never be forgotten, <div eID="gen12560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12561" type="x-p"/> I. That God brought Israel out of the house of bondage with a high hand and a stretched-out arm: <hi type="italic">Israel went out of Egypt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.114.1">v. 1</reference>. They did not steal out clandestinely, nor were they driven out, but fairly went out, marched out with all the marks of honour; they went out from a barbarous people, that had used them barbarously, from <hi type="italic">a people of a strange language,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.81.5">Ps. lxxxi. 5</reference>. The Israelites, it seems, preserved their own language pure among them, and cared not for learning the language of their oppressors. By this distinction from them they kept up an earnest of their deliverance. <div eID="gen12561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12562" type="x-p"/> II. That he himself framed their civil and sacred constitution (<reference osisRef="Ps.114.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Judah and Israel were his sanctuary, his dominion.</hi> When he delivered them out of the hand of their oppressors it was <hi type="italic">that they might serve him</hi> both <hi type="italic">in holiness and in righteousness,</hi> in the duties of religious worship and in obedience to the moral law, in their whole conversation. <hi type="italic">Let my people go, that they may serve me.</hi> In order to this, 1. He set up his sanctuary among them, in which he gave them the special tokens of his presence with them and promised to receive their homage and tribute. Happy are the people that have God's sanctuary among them (see <reference osisRef="Exod.25.8">Exod. xxv. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.26">Ezek. xxxvii. 26</reference>), much more those that, like Judah here, are his <hi type="italic">sanctuaries,</hi> his living temples, on whom <hi type="italic">Holiness to the Lord</hi> is written. 2. He set up his dominion among them, was himself their lawgiver and their judge, and their government was a theocracy: <hi type="italic">The Lord was their King.</hi> All the world is God's dominion, but Israel was so in a peculiar manner. What is God's sanctuary must be his dominion. Those only have the privileges of his house that submit to the laws of it; and for this end Christ has redeemed us that he might bring us into God's service and engage us for ever in it. <div eID="gen12562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12563" type="x-p"/> III. That the Red Sea was divided before them at their coming out of Egypt, both for their rescue and the ruin of their enemies; and the river Jordan, when they entered into Canaan, for their honour, and the confusion and terror of their enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.114.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">The sea saw it,</hi> saw there that <hi type="italic">Judah was God's sanctuary, and Israel his dominion, and</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">fled;</hi> for nothing could be more awful. It was this that <hi type="italic">drove Jordan back,</hi> and was an invincible dam to his streams; God was at the head of that people, and therefore they must give way to them, must make room for them, they must retire, contrary to their nature, when God speaks the word. To illustrate this the psalmist asks, in a poetical strain (<reference osisRef="Ps.114.5">v. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">What ailed thee, O thou sea! that thou fleddest?</hi> And furnishes the sea with an answer (<reference osisRef="Ps.114.7">v. 7</reference>); it was <hi type="italic">at the presence of the Lord.</hi> This is designed to express, 1. The reality of the miracle, that it was not by any power of nature, or from any natural cause, but it was <hi type="italic">at the presence of the Lord,</hi> who gave the word. 2. The mercy of the miracle: <hi type="italic">What ailed thee?</hi> Was it in a frolic? Was it only to amuse men? No; it was <hi type="italic">at the presence of the God of Jacob;</hi> it was in kindness to the Israel of God, <hi type="italic">for the salvation</hi> of that chosen people, that God was thus <hi type="italic">displeased against the rivers,</hi> and his <hi type="italic">wrath was against the sea,</hi> as the prophet speaks, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.8-Hab.3.13">Hab. iii. 8-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.10">Isa. li. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.11">lxvi. 11</reference>, &c. 3. The wonder and surprise of the miracle. Who would have thought of such a thing? Shall the course of nature be changed, and its fundamental laws dispensed with, to serve a turn for God's Israel? Well may the <hi type="italic">dukes of Edom be amazed</hi> and the <hi type="italic">mighty men of Moab tremble,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.15.15">Exod. xv. 15</reference>. 4. The honour hereby put upon Israel, who are taught to triumph over the sea, and Jordan, as unable to stand before them. Note, There is no sea, no Jordan, so deep, so broad, but, when God's time shall come for the redemption of his people, it shall be divided and driven back if it stand in their way. Apply this, (1.) To the planting of the Christian church in the world. What ailed Satan and the powers of darkness, that they trembled and truckled as they did? <reference osisRef="Mark.1.34">Mark i. 34</reference>. What ailed the heathen oracles, that they were silenced, struck dumb, struck dead? What ailed their idolatries and witchcrafts, that they died away before the gospel, and melted like snow before the sun? What ailed the persecutors and opposers of the gospel, that they gave up their cause, hid their guilty heads, and called to rocks and mountains for shelter? <reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Rev. vi. 15</reference>. It was <hi type="italic">at the presence of the Lord,</hi> and that power which went along with the gospel. (2.) To the work of grace in the heart. What turns the stream in a regenerate soul? What ails the lusts and corruptions, that they fly back, that the prejudices are removed and the whole man has become new? It is at the presence of God's Spirit that imaginations are <hi type="italic">cast down,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.5">2 Cor. x. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen12563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12564" type="x-p"/> IV. That the earth shook and trembled when God came down on Mount Sinai to give the law (<reference osisRef="Ps.114.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">The mountains skipped like rams, and</hi> then <hi type="italic">the little hills</hi> might well be excused if they skipped <hi type="italic">like lambs,</hi> either when they are frightened or when they sport themselves. The same power that fixed the fluid waters and made them stand still shook the stable mountains and made them tremble for all the powers of nature are under the check of the God of nature. Mountains and hills are, before God, but like rams and lambs; even the bulkiest and the most rocky are as manageable by him as <hi type="italic">they</hi> are by the shepherd. The trembling of the mountains before the Lord may shame the stupidity and obduracy of the children of men, who are not moved at the discoveries of his glory. The psalmist asks the mountains and hills what ailed them to skip thus; and he answers for them, as for the seas, it was <hi type="italic">at the presence of the Lord,</hi> before whom, not only those mountains, but the earth itself, may well tremble (<reference osisRef="Ps.114.7">v. 7</reference>), since it has lain under a curse for man's sin. See <reference osisRef="Ps.104.32">Ps. civ. 32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.64.3-Isa.64.4">Isa. lxiv. 3, 4</reference>. He that made the hills and mountains to skip thus can, when he pleases, dissipate the strength and spirit of the proudest of his enemies and make them tremble. <div eID="gen12564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12565" type="x-p"/> V. That God supplied them with water out of the rock, which followed them through the dry and sandy deserts. Well may the earth and all its inhabitants tremble before that God who <hi type="italic">turned the rock into a standing water</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.114.8">v. 8</reference>), and what cannot he do who did that? The same almighty power that turned waters into a rock to be a wall to Israel (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.22">Exod. xiv. 22</reference>) turned the rock into waters to be a well to Israel: as they were protected, so they were provided for, by miracles, standing miracles; for such was the standing water, that fountain of waters into which the rock, the flinty rock, was turned, <hi type="italic">and that rock was Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.4">1 Cor. x. 4</reference>. For he is a fountain of living waters to his Israel, from whom they receive grace for grace.  <chapter eID="Ps.114"/> <div eID="gen12565" type="x-p"/>

entries.1a0931390ed56ead940f8b97f3327c8bb7a9126c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6830"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 114</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.114.1-Ps.114.8">Psa 114:1-8</reference>. The writer briefly and beautifully celebrates God's former care of His people, to whose benefit nature was miraculously made to contribute.</title> <div sID="gen10490" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6830"/><hi type="bold">1-4. of strange language--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Ps.81.5">Psa 81:5</reference>). <div eID="gen10490" type="x-p"/>
entries.5823d6389748bbd9978620148dafc2961e4f7253: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6832"/><div sID="gen10492" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6832"/>5-8. The questions place the implied answers in a more striking form. <div eID="gen10492" type="x-p"/>

entries.da14fc7bb8ccf4862687d6cc2078072d83b0e526: <div eID="gen22534" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22535" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22536" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22536" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22535" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22537" type="x-p"/> Miracles wrought at the exodus of the Israelites from Egypt, at the Red Sea, and at Jordan, <reference osisRef="Psa.114.1-Psa.114.6">Psa 114:1-6</reference>; and at the rock of Horeb, <reference osisRef="Psa.114.7">Psa 114:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.114.8">Psa 114:8</reference>. <div eID="gen22537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22538" type="x-p"/> This Psalm has no title. The word Hallelujah is prefixed in all the Versions except the Chaldee and Syriac. It seems like a fragment, or a part of another Psalm. In many MSS. it is only the beginning of the following; both making but one Psalm in all the Versions, except the Chaldee. It is elegantly and energetically composed; but begins and ends very abruptly, if we separate it from the following. As to the author of this Psalm, there have been various opinions; some have given the honor of it to Shadrach, Meshech, and Abed-nego; others to Esther; and others, to Mordecai. <div eID="gen22538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22539" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22540" type="x-p"/> A people of strange language - This may mean no more than a barbarous people; a people whom they did not know, and who did not worship their God. But it is a fact that the language of the Egyptians in the time of Joseph was so different from that of the Hebrews that they could not understand each other. See <reference osisRef="Psa.81.5">Psa 81:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.42.23">Gen 42:23</reference>. <div eID="gen22540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22541" type="x-p"/> The Chaldee has here מעמי ברבראי meammey barbarey, which gives reason to believe that the word is Chaldee, or more properly Phoenician. See this word fully explained in the note on <reference osisRef="Act.28.2">Act 28:2</reference> (note). My old Psalter understood the word as referring to the religious state of the Egyptians: In gangyng of Isrel oute of Egipt, of the house of Jocob fra hethen folke.
entries.94143445ad7143cb734a1099a0f2c2b463c95f27: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen22541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22542" type="x-p"/> Judah was his sanctuary - He set up his true worship among the Jews, and took them for his peculiar people. <div eID="gen22542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22543" type="x-p"/> And Israel his dominion - These words are a proof, were there none other, that this Psalm was composed after the days of David, and after the division of the tribes, for then the distinction of Israel and Judah took place.
entries.4b291dc1d552915fff85ffdefa09cfd3d3e85f27: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen22543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22544" type="x-p"/> The sea saw it, and fled - Mr. Addison has properly observed (see Spect. No. 461) that the author of this Psalm designedly works for effect, in pointing out the miraculous driving back the Red Sea and the river Jordan, and the commotion of the hills and mountains, without mentioning any agent. At last, when the reader sees the sea rapidly retiring from the shore, Jordan retreating to its source, and the mountains and hills running away like a flock of affrighted sheep, that the passage of the Israelites might be every where uninterrupted; then the cause of all is suddenly introduced, and the presence of God in his grandeur solves every difficulty.
entries.476490fe041e461d2745565c31dee02e02a5791b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen22544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22545" type="x-p"/> What ailed thee, O thou sea - The original is very abrupt; and the prosopopoeia, or personification very fine and expressive: - <div eID="gen22545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22546" type="x-p"/> What to thee, O sea, that thou fleddest away! <div eID="gen22546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22547" type="x-p"/> O Jordan, that thou didst roll back! <div eID="gen22547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22548" type="x-p"/> Ye mountains, that ye leaped like rams! <div eID="gen22548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22549" type="x-p"/> And ye hills, like the young of the fold! <div eID="gen22549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22550" type="x-p"/> After these very sublime interrogations, God appears; and the psalmist proceeds as if answering his own questions: - <div eID="gen22550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22551" type="x-p"/> At the appearance of the Lord, O earth, thou didst tremble; <div eID="gen22551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22552" type="x-p"/> At the appearance of the strong God of Jacob. <div eID="gen22552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22553" type="x-p"/> Converting the rock into a pool of waters; <div eID="gen22553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22554" type="x-p"/> The granite into water springs. <div eID="gen22554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22555" type="x-p"/> I know the present Hebrew text reads חולי chuli, "tremble thou," in the imperative; but almost all the Versions understood the word in past tense, and read as if the psalmist was answering his own questions, as stated in the translation above. "Tremble thou, O earth." As if he had said, Thou mayest well tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob.
entries.7c8132f8d49048dac3bcc7131f1659ccf2f35bfa: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen22555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22556" type="x-p"/> The flint - I have translated חלמיש challamish, Granite; for such is the rock of Horeb, a piece of which now lies before me. <div eID="gen22556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22557" type="x-p"/> This short and apparently imperfect Psalm, for elegance and sublimity, yields to few in the whole book. <div eID="gen22557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22558" type="x-p"/> It is so well translated in the old Psalter, that I think I shall gratify the reader by laying it before him. <reference osisRef="Psa.114.1">Psa 114:1</reference> In gangyng of Isrel oute of Egipt,Of the house of Jacob fra hethen folke. <reference osisRef="Psa.114.2">Psa 114:2</reference> Made is Jude his halawyngIsrel might of hym. <reference osisRef="Psa.114.3">Psa 114:3</reference> The se sawe and fled,Jurdan turned is agayne; <reference osisRef="Psa.114.4">Psa 114:4</reference> Hawes gladed als wethers,And hilles als lambes of schepe. <reference osisRef="Psa.114.5">Psa 114:5</reference> What is to the se, that thou fled?And thou Jordane that thou ert turned agayne? <reference osisRef="Psa.114.6">Psa 114:6</reference> Hawes gladded als wethers?And hils als lambs of schepe. <reference osisRef="Psa.114.7">Psa 114:7</reference> Fra the face of Lorde styrde is the erth,Fra the face of God of Jabob; <reference osisRef="Psa.114.8">Psa 114:8</reference> That turnes the stane in stank of waters,And roche in wels of waters. <div eID="gen22558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22559" type="x-p"/> And, as a still more ancient specimen of our language, I shall insert the Anglo-Saxon, with a literal reading, line for line, as near to the Saxon as possible, merely to show the affinity of the languages. <reference osisRef="Psa.114.1">Psa 114:1</reference> On outgang Israel of Egypt,House Jacob of folk foreigners; <reference osisRef="Psa.114.2">Psa 114:2</reference> Made is Jacob holyness his;Israel andweald (government) his. <reference osisRef="Psa.114.3">Psa 114:3</reference> Sea saw, and flew!Jordan turned underback! <reference osisRef="Psa.114.4">Psa 114:4</reference> Mounts they fain (rejoiced) so (as) rams,And burghs (hillocks) so (as) lamb - sheep. <reference osisRef="Psa.114.5">Psa 114:5</reference> What is the sea, that thou flew?And thou river for that thou turned is underback? <reference osisRef="Psa.114.6">Psa 114:6</reference> Mounts ye fained (rejoiced) so so rams;And hills so so lambs - sheep. <reference osisRef="Psa.114.7">Psa 114:7</reference> From sight Lord's stirred is earth;From sight God of Jacob. <reference osisRef="Psa.114.8">Psa 114:8</reference> Who turned stone in mere waters;And cliffs in wells waters. <div eID="gen22559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22560" type="x-p"/> I have retained some words above in nearly their Saxon form, because they still exist in our old writers; or, with little variation, in those of the present day: - <reference osisRef="Psa.114.2">Psa 114:2</reference> Andweald, government. Hence weal and wealth, commonweal or wealth; the general government, that which produces the welfare of the country. <reference osisRef="Psa.114.4">Psa 114:4</reference> Faegnodon, fained - desired fervently, felt delight in expectation. <reference osisRef="Psa.114.4">Psa 114:4</reference> Burgh, a hill - a mound or heap of earth, such as was raised up over the dead. Hence a barrow; and hence the word bury, to inhume the dead. <reference osisRef="Psa.114.8">Psa 114:8</reference> Mere, or meer, a large pool of water, a lake, a lough, still in use in the north of England. Gentlemen's ponds, or large sheets of water so called; and hence Winander-mere, a large lake in Westmoreland. Mere also signifies limit or boundary; hence the Mersey, the river which divides Lancashire from Cheshire, and serves as a boundary to both counties. The mere that spreads itself out to the sea. <div eID="gen22560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22561" type="x-p"/> Instead of cludas, which signifies rocks, one MS. has clyf, which signifies a craggy mountain or broken rock. <div eID="gen22561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22562" type="x-p"/> The reader will see from this specimen how much of our ancient language still remains in the present; and perhaps also how much, in his opinion, we have amplified and improved our mother tongue.  <chapter eID="Ps.114"/> <div eID="gen22562" type="x-p"/>

entries.eff7e0b4a35d089b0a426fee3a88d30e1a7d17bd: <div eID="gen10090" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Commotion of Nature before God the Redeemer out of Egypt</title> <div sID="gen10091" type="x-p"/> To the side of the general Hallelujah <reference osisRef="Ps.113.1-Ps.113.9">Psa 113:1-9</reference> comes an historical one, which is likewise adorned in <reference osisRef="Ps.114.8">Psa 114:8</reference> with the <hi type="italic">Chirek compaginis</hi>, and still further with <hi type="italic">Cholem compaginis</hi>, and is the festival Psalm of the eighth Passover day in the Jewish ritual. The deeds of God at the time of the Exodus are here brought together to form a picture in miniature which is as majestic as it is charming. There are four tetrastichs, which pass by with the swiftness of a bird as it were with four flappings of its wings. The church sings this Psalm in a <hi type="italic">tonus peregrinus</hi> distinct from the eight Psalm-tones.
entries.f8a3b4375efcaa2667bfbaf3a462755bfde8cfed: <reference osisRef="Ps.114.1-Ps.114.4">Psa 114:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen10091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10092" type="x-p"/> Egypt is called עם לעז (from לעז, cogn. לעג, לעה), because the people spoke a language unintelligible to Israel (<reference osisRef="Ps.81.6">Psa 81:6</reference>), and as it were a stammering language. The lxx, and just so the Targum, renders ἐκ λαοῦ βαρβάρου (from the Sanscrit <hi type="italic">barbaras</hi>, just as onomatopoetic as <hi type="italic">balbus</hi>, cf. Fleischer in Levy’s <hi type="italic">Chaldäisches Wörterbuch</hi>, i. 420). The redeemed nation is called <hi type="italic">Judah</hi>, inasmuch as God made it His sanctuary (קדשׁ) by setting up His sanctuary (מקדּשׁ, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.17">Exo 15:17</reference>) in the midst of it, for Jerusalem (<hi type="italic">el ḳuds</hi>) as Benjamitish Judaean, and from the time of David was accounted directly as Judaean. In so far, however, as He made this people His kingdom (ממשׁלותיו, an amplificative plural with <hi type="italic">Mem pathachatum</hi>), by placing Himself in the relation of King (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.5">Deu 33:5</reference>) to the people of possession which by a revealed law He established characteristically as His own, it is called <hi type="italic">Israel</hi>. 1 The predicate takes the form ותּהי, for peoples together with country and city are represented as feminine (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.8.5">Jer 8:5</reference>). The foundation of that new beginning in connection with the history of redemption was laid amidst majestic wonders, inasmuch as nature was brought into service, co-operating and sympathizing in the work (cf. Psa 77:15.). The dividing of the sea opens, and the dividing of the Jordan closes, the journey through the desert to Canaan. The sea stood aside, Jordan halted and was dammed up on the north in order that the redeemed people might pass through. And in the middle, between these great wonders of the Exodus from Egypt and the entrance into Canaan, arises the not less mighty wonder of the giving of the Law: the skipping of the mountains like rams, of the ills like בּני־צאן, i.e., lambs (Wisd. 19:9), depicts the quaking of Sinai and its environs (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.18">Exo 19:18</reference>, cf. <hi type="italic">supra</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.9">Psa 68:9</reference>, and on the figure <reference osisRef="Ps.29.6">Psa 29:6</reference>).
entries.c54366dd7cf241ed2dfc69aa4bb2d5bba4005a3f: <reference osisRef="Ps.114.5-Ps.114.8">Psa 114:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen10092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10093" type="x-p"/> The poet, when he asks, “What aileth thee, O sea, that thou fleest...?” lives and moves in this olden time as a contemporary, or the present and the olden time as it were flow together to his mind; hence the answer he himself gives to the question propounded takes the form of a triumphant mandate. The Lord, the God of Jacob, thus mighty in wondrous works, it is before whom the earth must tremble. אדון does not take the article because it finds its completion in the following יעקב (אלוהּ); it is the same <hi type="italic">epizeuxis</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Ps.113.8">Psa 113:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.3">Psa 94:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.96.7">Psa 96:7</reference>, Psa 96:13. ההפכי has the constructive <hi type="italic">ı̂</hi> out of the genitival relation; and in למעינו in this relation we have the constructive <hi type="italic">ô</hi>, which as a rule occurs only in the genitival combination, with the exception of this passage and בּנו באר, Num 24:3, Num 24:15 (not, however, in <reference osisRef="Prov.13.4">Pro 13:4</reference>, “his, the sluggard’s, soul”), found only in the name for wild animals חיתו־ארץ, which occurs frequently, and first of all in Gen 1:24. The expression calls to mind Psa 107:35. הצּוּר is taken from <reference osisRef="Exod.17.6">Exo 17:6</reference>; and חלּמישׁ (lxx τὴν ἀκρότομον, that which is rugged, abrupt)<note placement="foot">One usually compares Arab. <hi type="italic">chlnbûs , chalnabûs</hi> the Karaite lexicographer Abraham ben David writes חלמבוס]; but this obsolete word, as a compound from Arab. <hi type="italic">chls</hi>, to be black-grey, and Arab. <hi type="italic">chnbs</hi>, to be hard, may originally signify a hard black-grey stone, whereas חלמישׁ looks like a mingling of the verbal stems Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥms</hi>, to be hard, and Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥls</hi>, to be black-brown (as Arab. <hi type="italic">jlmûd</hi>, a detached block of rock, is of the verbal stems Arab. <hi type="italic">jld</hi>, to be hard, and Arab. <hi type="italic">jmd</hi>, to be massive). In Hauran the doors of the houses and the window-shutters are called Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥalasat</hi> when they consist of a massive slab of dolerite, probably from their blackish hue. Perhaps חלמישׁ is the ancient name for basalt; and in connection with the hardness of this form of rock, which resembles a mass of cast metal, the breaking through of springs is a great miracle. - Wetzstein. For other views vid., on <reference osisRef="Isa.49.21">Isa 49:21</reference>; Isa 50:7.</note> stands, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.8.15">Deu 8:15</reference>, poetically for סלע, Num 20:11, for it is these two histories of the giving of water to which the poet points back. But why to these in particular? The causing of water to gush forth out of the flinty rock is a practical proof of unlimited omnipotence and of the grace which converts death into life. Let the earth then tremble before the Lord, the God of Jacob. It has already trembled before Him, and before Him let it tremble. For that which He has been He still ever is; and as He came once, He will come again.  <chapter eID="Ps.114"/> <div eID="gen10093" type="x-p"/>

entries.49c54d615f3330e58d8263c9625a8d8239eb7115:
PSALM 114
This psalm contains a short account of that deliverance by which God, in bringing his people out of Egypt: and conducting them to the promised inheritance, gave a proof of his power and grace which ought to be held in everlasting remembrance. The design of that wonderful deliverance was, that the seed of Abraham might yield themselves wholly to God, who, receiving them by a gracious act of adoption, purposed that they should be to him a holy and peculiar people.
“The exodus of Israel from Egypt, with some of its most remarkable accompanying and consequent miracles, are, in this brief psalm, commemorated in the boldest style of poetry, with personifications, indeed, of inanimate nature of the utmost daring and sublimity, in ‘thoughts that breathe, and words that burn.’” — Drake’s Harp of Judah.
Psalm 114:1-4
1. When Israel went out from Egypt, and the house of Jacob from a barbarous people;
The word לעז, loez, which Calvin renders, a barbarous people, is translated, in our English Bible, “a people of strange language.” His version is supported by many authorities. The word is frequently found, in the sense he attaches to it, in Rabbinical works, and is so understood here by the Chaldee paraphrast, who has ברבראי, and by the LXX., who have βαρβάρου. The root of these terms, as well as the Latin word for barbarous, is probably the Hebrew בר, out, or without, redoubled; and so it signifies, to a Jew, any man of another nation. According to Parkhurst, the word, instead of signifying a barbarous or foreign language or pronunciation, seems rather to refer to the violence of the Egyptians towards the Israelites, or the barbarity of their behavior, which, he observes, was more to the Psalmist’s purpose than the barbarity of their language, even supposing the reality of the latter in the time of Moses. — See his Lexicon on לעז. Horsley reads, “a tyrannical people.”
2. Judah was for his
“There is a peculiar beauty in the conduct of this psalm, in that the author utterly conceals the presence of God in the beginning of it, and rather lets a possessive pronoun (i.e. His) go without a substantive, than he will so much as mention any thing of Divinity there; because, if God had appeared before, there could be no wonder why the mountains should leap, and the sea retire; therefore, that this convulsion of nature may be brought in with due surprise, his name is not mentioned till afterwards, and then, with a very agreeable turn of thought, God is introduced at once with all majesty ” — Spectator, volume 6, No. 461. If, however, the last two words of the preceding psalm, הללו-יה, Halelu-yah, Praise ye Jehovah, are the title to this psalm, the antecedent to his is supplied.
holiness, Israel for his dominions. 3. The sea saw, and fled:
In the Hebrew there is no pronoun after saw; nor is any inserted in the Septuagint and Arabic versions, or in the Chaldee. In our English Bible, it is inserted, and him in the Syriac version; but the sentence is certainly much more sublime without any such supplement.
Jordan was turned backward. 4. The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills as the lambs of the flock.
 
1 When Israel went out from Egypt That exodus being a remarkable pledge and symbol of God’s love for the children of Abraham, it is not surprising that it should be so frequently called to remembrance. In the beginning of the psalm, the prophet informs us that the people whom God purchased at so great a price are no more their own. The opinion of certain expositors, that at that time the tribe of Judah was consecrated to the service of God, according to what is said in Exodus 19:6, and 1 Peter 2:9, appears to me foreign to the prophet’s design. All doubt about the matter is removed by what is immediately subjoined, God’s taking Israel under his rule, which is simply a repetition of the same sentiment in other words. Judah being the most powerful and numerous of all the tribes, and occupying the chief place among them, here takes the precedency of the rest of the people. At the same time, it is very evident that the honor which is in a peculiar manner ascribed to them, belongs equally to the whole body of the people.
“Judah represents here the whole people of Israel, as Joseph does, in Psalm 81:6. The reason assigned by Kimchi for this use of יהודה here is, that at the time of the departure from Egypt, Judah was considered the head or chief of the tribes; see Genesis 49:8-10. This, however, is mere conjecture. If it be necessary to assign reasons for the distinction here conferred on this tribe, I should mention as one:, that the ark was kept in the region occupied by the descendants of Judah, and, as another, that from him the Messiah was to spring.” — Phillips.
When God is said to be sanctified, it must be understood that the prophet is speaking after the manner of men, because, in himself, God is incapable of increase or diminution. Judah is called his holiness,
God’s holiness being often taken for the keeping his promise sacred or inviolate, as in Psalm 102:9, when, reference being made to the immutability of his covenant, it is added, “holy [as in another respect, reverend] is his name;” some, as Hammond and Cresswell, suppose that the meaning here is, that God’s dealings towards Judah — the people of the Jews, were a demonstration of his faithfulness in performing his promise made to Abraham long before.
and Israel his dominion,
Hammond reads, “And Israel his power,” by which he understands that Israel was an instance of his power; that God, in his acting for Israel, declared his omnipotence most signally.
because his holy majesty, which hitherto had been little known, secured the veneration of all who had witnessed the displays of his incredible power. In delivering his people, God erected a kingdom for himself and procured respect for his sacred name; if then they do not constantly reflect upon such a remarkable instance of his kindness, their insensibility is totally inexcusable.
